<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README contents, this project is a full‐stack system for creating secure peer-to-peer networks based on WireGuard. It implements both the networking agent (client) that runs on each participating machine and several centralized services (management, signal, and relay) to maintain network state, coordinate connection negotiations (using Pion ICE/STUN/TURN), and to provide fallback connectivity when direct peer-to-peer links cannot be established.

Here’s how you can design an accurate and detailed system architecture diagram tailored for this project:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Client/Agent: Represented by the extensive “client” directory. This component is responsible for managing the WireGuard tunnel, handling local firewall adjustments, local DNS, interface configuration, and for using Pion ICE for candidate discovery.
   • Management Service: Found under the “management” directory. This service manages the network state (peer IPs, access policies, authentication, and authorization), provides a centralized API (both REST and gRPC endpoints as suggested by the subdirectories), and interfaces with the Admin UI.
   • Signal Service: Represented by the “signal” directory. This service is used by clients to exchange encrypted peer-to-peer candidate details (using WebRTC ICE) to negotiate connectivity.
   • Relay Service: Present as the “relay” directory. It serves as the TURN fallback when NAT traversal fails. It relays traffic between peers using secure tunnels.
   • Additional Supporting Components: Although not “services” per se, include components such as:
       - DNS and Encryption modules (directories like dns/ and encryption/) that support service-specific functions.
       - Infrastructure/Deployment modules (infrastructure_files, Dockerfiles in .devcontainer, client Dockerfiles, etc.) which indicate containerized deployment and environment configuration.
       - Auxiliary libraries and utilities (sharedsock, util, formatter, version) that support common functions across the platform.

2. Define Relationships and Data Flows:
   • Draw directional arrows showing that:
       - Every Agent (client) initiates a connection to the Management Service to report its state, receive configuration updates, and to register for access control.
       - The Agent also communicates with the Signal Service to exchange connection candidates necessary for establishing a direct peer-to-peer connection.
       - In case the direct connection fails (or due to strict NAT rules), a fallback mechanism is activated where the Agent uses the Relay Service as a TURN server, establishing an indirect WireGuard tunnel.
       - The Management Service may also interact with external Identity Providers (as suggested by the IdP directories under management) and exposes REST and gRPC APIs to the UI or external integration components.
       - Underlying DNS and security modules (encryption, firewall rules) are invoked within both the Client and Management Services.
   
3. Highlight Architectural Patterns and Technology Stack:
   • The system follows a microservices-like separation even though they are part of the same code repository:
       - Enforcement of decentralized agent functionality vs. centralized management.
       - Separation of concerns: Connection negotiations (Signal), network control (Management), and data tunneling (Client and Relay).
   • Emphasize that the client component is written in Go (observing numerous .go files and go.mod) and uses libraries such as WireGuard, Pion ICE for candidate discovery, and possibly GRPC for management communication.
   • Note integration of containerization (Dockerfiles, docker-compose templates) to support deployment in multiple environments.
   • The project also supports various platforms (Linux, macOS, Windows, mobile) which should be indicated along the client component.

4. Diagram Guidelines:
   • Represent each key component as a clearly labeled node:
       - Label nodes “Agent/Client”, “Management Service”, “Signal Service”, and “Relay Service”.
       - Optionally, also have nodes for “DNS Module”, “Encryption & Access Control”, and “UI/API” for admin management.
   • Use directional arrows to reflect the communication flows:
       - For example, an arrow from “Agent” to “Management Service” labeled “state update / configuration” and from “Agent” to “Signal Service” labeled “connection negotiation (ICE candidates)”.
       - Arrows from “Agent” to “Relay Service” under fallback conditions.
   • Consider using different colors or shapes to distinguish between backend services (Management, Signal, Relay) and client-side components.
   • If helpful, layer the diagram into tiers, such as showing client devices in one tier, and the server-side services (Management/Signal/Relay) in another tier, with additional indication of external interactions (such as integration with IdP providers or external STUN/TURN servers like Coturn).
   • Annotate with the major technologies (Go, WireGuard, Pion ICE) and list protocols (REST/gRPC, WebRTC, NAT traversal) where appropriate.

5. Tailor the Diagram to the Project:
   • Since NetBird is a full-stack network security platform, emphasize the clear separation between:
       - The distributed agents that reside on user endpoints (which handle local networking and firewall configuration).
       - The centralized control and coordination provided by the management service along with authentication, API interaction, and policy enforcement.
       - The communication layer between peers (handled by the signal service) and the fallback connection provided by the relay service.
   • Make sure that every component shows its role in the overall “connect, secure, and automate” flow.
   • Do not hesitate to split sub-components within the management service (e.g., HTTP API, auth, and caching modules) if further detail is required, but a high-level diagram that shows clear boundaries is most effective.

By following these instructions, you should have a detailed and clear diagram that accurately represents NetBird’s architecture, its core components, and the interplay between modern networking protocols, a secure tunneling technology like WireGuard, and related management and signaling services. Be sure to clearly annotate, label, and use directional arrows and color codes to make the relationships intuitive at a glance.
</explanation>
